column1: Does kube-proxy process every packet sent to a Service?
column2: No — it only programs iptables/nftables/IPVS rules; the kernel handles all actual packet forwarding using those rules

column1: What replaced the deprecated Endpoints API?
column2: EndpointSlices — multiple slices per Service (up to 100 endpoints each), with dual-stack support and readiness/topology tracking the old API lacked

column1: For a Service WITH a selector, is its EndpointSlice self-healing if deleted?
column2: Yes — the endpointslice-controller continuously reconciles it against the selector and currently-Ready pods, and recreates it almost immediately

column1: For a selectorless Service, is its manually-created EndpointSlice self-healing?
column2: No — nothing reconciles it automatically; you're fully responsible for keeping it accurate yourself

column1: Does deleting a kube-proxy pod interrupt existing Service routing on that node?
column2: No — the iptables rules it already programmed stay in place; kube-proxy isn't in the data path, only the rule-programming path

column1: Why does kube-proxy run on the control-plane node despite the scheduling taint there?
column2: It's a DaemonSet with its own toleration for the control-plane taint — taints only block pods that don't explicitly tolerate them

column1: What does Ready: false on an EndpointSlice entry mean for that pod?
column2: It's excluded from load balancing — matching the Service's selector alone isn't enough, only Ready endpoints receive traffic

column1: How does iptables achieve roughly equal load distribution across 3 pod endpoints?
column2: Cascading statistic-mode probabilities: 0.333 for the first, 0.500 of the remainder for the second, everything left for the third — netting out to roughly 1/3 each

column1: If every backend pod returns identical response text, does that prove load balancing isn't working?
column2: No — it just means you can't observe it from response content; distinguishing data per pod (like an injected pod name) is needed to actually verify routing

column1: What kube-proxy modes exist on Linux, and what is ipvs's current status?
column2: iptables, nftables, and ipvs — ipvs was formally deprecated in Kubernetes v1.35; nftables is the currently recommended mode for new clusters on modern kernels
